4.0.big: The cell is the basic unit of life. Every organism is one cell or many, and every cell comes from another cell.
points: Cells come in two big types: prokaryotes (simple, no nucleus) and eukaryotes (with a nucleus and organelles).

4.1.big: Cells are too small to see without a microscope, and studying them led to the cell theory.
points: Light microscope: uses light, can view living cells, magnifies about 400–1,000×, and often needs stains for contrast.
Electron microscope: uses electrons, far higher magnification and resolution, but the specimen is dead. Scanning EM shows 3-D surfaces. Transmission EM shows inside structures.

History: Hooke named "cells" (cork), van Leeuwenhoek saw living microbes, Schleiden (plants) and Schwann (animals) proposed that all living things are made of cells, and Virchow said all cells come from existing cells.

Cell theory (the unified cell theory): all living things are made of cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and new cells come from existing cells. (That last part is why sterilizing works: no cells, no new cells.)

4.2.big: Prokaryotes (bacteria and archaea) are small and simple: no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles.
points: All cells have a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, and DNA.
Prokaryote DNA sits in a nucleoid region. Extras: a cell wall (peptidoglycan in bacteria), capsule, fimbriae (for sticking to surfaces), a flagellum (for swimming), and plasmids.
Small cells have a high surface-area-to-volume ratio, so nutrients and waste diffuse in and out quickly. That ratio is why cells stay small.
4.2.tip: As a cell gets bigger, its volume grows faster than its surface, so it can't feed itself through its membrane anymore.

4.3.big: A eukaryotic cell has a nucleus and many organelles, each doing a specialized job.
points: Plasma membrane: a phospholipid bilayer that controls what goes in and out. Some cells add folds (microvilli) for absorption.
Cytoplasm = everything between membrane and nucleus. The fluid part is the cytosol.
Nucleus: holds DNA as chromatin (which condenses into chromosomes for division), surrounded by a double nuclear envelope and filled with nucleoplasm. The nucleolus builds ribosomes.
Ribosomes: make proteins. Found in all cells.
Mitochondria: cellular respiration, making ATP. Double membrane with folds (cristae), their own DNA. Muscle cells have lots.
Peroxisomes: break down fatty acids and toxins, making and then destroying hydrogen peroxide.
Vesicles and vacuoles: membrane sacs for storage and transport.

Plant cells add a cell wall (cellulose), chloroplasts (photosynthesis with chlorophyll; double membrane, own DNA), and a big central vacuole (water pressure; also does lysosome-like digestion). Animal cells have lysosomes and a centrosome (centrioles).

4.4.big: The endomembrane system is the cell's factory and shipping department: the ER, Golgi, lysosomes, vesicles, nuclear envelope and plasma membrane.
points: Rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER): covered in ribosomes. It makes and folds proteins headed for membranes or export, and is continuous with the nuclear envelope.
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER): no ribosomes. It makes lipids and steroid hormones, detoxifies, and stores calcium.
Golgi apparatus: receives vesicles from the ER at its cis face, modifies and sorts proteins, and ships them out from its trans face.
Protein path: ribosome on the RER → vesicle → Golgi → vesicle → plasma membrane (secretion) or lysosome.
Lysosomes: bags of digestive enzymes that break down food, old organelles and pathogens (very busy in macrophages).
Proteins made on free ribosomes stay in the cytosol and skip the Golgi.

4.5.big: The cytoskeleton is a network of protein fibers that gives the cell shape, moves things around, and lets cells move.
points: Microfilaments (actin, the thinnest): muscle contraction (with myosin), cell crawling, and cell division pinching. They assemble and disassemble quickly.
Intermediate filaments: strong ropes that bear tension and hold the nucleus in place. Not involved in movement.
Microtubules (tubulin, the thickest): tracks for vesicles, pulling chromosomes apart in division, and building centrioles, cilia and flagella. Drugs that block them stop cancer cells from dividing.
Cilia (short and many, singular cilium) and flagella (long and few) share a 9 + 2 microtubule arrangement. Centrioles have a 9 × 3 arrangement.

4.6.big: Cells connect to and communicate with neighbors through the extracellular matrix and cell junctions.
points: Extracellular matrix (animals): mostly collagen and proteoglycans. It links to the cytoskeleton through membrane proteins, so outside signals can change what's inside.
Tight junctions: seal neighboring cells so nothing leaks between them (gut lining).
Desmosomes: spot-welds that hold cells together under stress (skin, heart and muscle).
Gap junctions: protein channels that let ions and small molecules pass between animal cells (heart muscle signals).
Plasmodesma (plural plasmodesmata): channels through plant cell walls connecting neighboring cells.

1.why: Stains add contrast so parts stand out.

2.why: The cell is the basic unit of life.

3.why: Cell theory: all living things are made of cells.

6.why: Seeing that plant and animal cells share nuclei and organelles helped show all life is made of cells.

9.why: Both have cytoplasm, but prokaryotes lack a nucleus.

10.why: Smaller cells have a higher surface-to-volume ratio.

11.why: The nucleoplasm is enclosed by the double-membrane nuclear envelope.

13.why: The plant vacuole does the lysosome's digesting.

16.why: DNA is in the nucleus and the mitochondria.

17.why: The SER makes lipids, including steroid hormones.

18.why: After the ribosome, proteins go into the ER to be modified.

20.why: Microfilaments and microtubules rapidly build and break down.

21.why: Intermediate filaments only bear tension. They don't move things.

24.why: Gap junctions are protein channels between cells.

27.why: Cells only come from existing cells, so killing them (sterilizing) prevents growth.

28.why: Light: keeps cells alive but lower resolution. Electron: high detail but costly and kills the specimen.

29.why: Plants still need mitochondria to break down sugar for ATP.

30.why: Light microscopes can watch living cells grow.

31.why: Without a wall, water rushes in and the cells may burst.

32.why: Surface-to-volume ratio limits how big a cell can get.

33.why: The wall protects against osmotic pressure, preventing bursting.

34.why: Bacteria use their plasma membrane for these reactions.

35.why: Both have double membranes, make ATP and have DNA. Mitochondria have cristae. Chloroplasts have thylakoids, grana and stroma.

36.why: Yes. The nuclear envelope is continuous with the rough ER.

37.why: Free-ribosome proteins skip the Golgi and stay in the cytosol.

39.why: No microtubules = no spindle = chromosomes can't separate, so division stops.

40.why: Cilia are short and many. Flagella are long and few.

42.why: Yes. Exposed collagen in damaged vessels triggers platelets to clump, so faulty collagen affects clotting.

43.why: Gap junctions connect animal cells. Plasmodesmata connect plant cells through their walls.

44.why: Simple prokaryotes like archaea came first, in a low-oxygen world.

45.why: Bacteria have no hard parts, so their fossils keep little detail to analyze.

46.why: The bigger cell B has a smaller surface-to-volume ratio.

47.why: Cube: volume 1, surface 6. Sphere: volume about 0.52, surface about 3.14. The cube wins both.

49.why: A cell must be big enough to hold everything needed for life.

51.why: All life shares the same phospholipid-and-protein membrane layout.

52.why: Endurance muscles need lots of ATP: mitochondria.

55.why: It has no membrane-bound organelles, so it's a bacterium despite its size.

56.why: ER → vesicles → Golgi → vesicles → out of the cell.

57.why: The matrix links (through membrane proteins) to the cytoskeleton.

58.why: Only flagella move bacteria. Fimbriae are for sticking.

59.why: Microvilli add surface area for absorbing nutrients.
